problemText: Which of the following is a physical characteristic of a place?
choices: A weekly market where farmers sell vegetables
A steep mountain valley that runs through the region
A workshop where people build wooden boats
A festival that people hold every spring
hints: Physical characteristics come from the land or weather, not from what people built or do.
Would this feature still be there if nobody ever lived in the place?

problemText: Read this description of a town called Millbrook: 'Millbrook sits at the edge of a wide river on flat land. Every morning, workers load grain onto boats to send downriver.' Which statement correctly explains why this description is complete?
choices: It mentions the flat land and the river, which are two different physical characteristics.
It includes both a landform and a climate pattern that define the town.
It names both a physical characteristic (the river and flat land) and a human characteristic (loading grain onto boats).
It provides three separate details, which is always enough to describe any place.
hints: A complete description must pass both questions: does it name a physical characteristic AND a human characteristic?
Loading grain is something people do—that is a human characteristic. What natural feature of the land does the description mention?

problemText: A student describes a place called Highpeak as follows: 'Highpeak has cold, snowy winters and mild summers. The streets are lined with buildings painted in bright colors, and artisans create crafts in small studios.' A classmate says the description is incomplete. Is the classmate right or wrong, and why?
choices: The classmate is wrong because the description includes four different details.
The classmate is wrong because it mentions both the climate and the painted buildings.
The classmate is right because the description mentions climate but only human details about buildings.
The classmate is right because the description does not name any landforms.
hints: Check both questions: does it name a physical characteristic (landform OR climate)? Does it name a human characteristic (building OR activity)?
Climate counts as a physical characteristic. Does the description include any natural landforms like a mountain, plain, or coastline?

problemText: Two geographers are describing the same town, Willowport. Geographer A says: 'Willowport has a wide harbor and mild, rainy winters. Fishing boats fill the docks every day, and the people hold a festival each summer.' Geographer B says: 'Willowport lies on a bay with sandy beaches. The townspeople run a busy port with warehouses full of traded goods.' Which geographer has provided a complete description, and why?
choices: Geographer A has provided a complete description because both a climate detail and a human activity are named, while Geographer B mentions only buildings and no natural features.
Geographer B has provided a complete description because it identifies both a landform (bay and beaches) and human characteristic (port operations and warehouses).
Both geographers have provided equally complete descriptions because each mentions physical features and human activities in similar amounts.
Neither geographer's description is complete because Geographer A omits landforms and Geographer B omits any mention of climate or weather patterns.
hints: Apply the two-question check to each description separately. Geographer A names the harbor (landform), winters (climate), fishing boats and festivals (activity). Geographer B names the bay and beaches (landforms) and warehouses (building).
Does Geographer B's description include any mention of the town's climate or weather pattern? Is that required for completeness?

problemText: A geography student says: 'A place cannot have a complete description using only one landform and one activity. You need at least one landform, one climate detail, and one building to describe any place properly.' Is this reasoning correct? Explain your answer using an example from the lesson.
choices: The reasoning is correct because the lesson teaches that you must have at least three kinds of detail to describe a place.

The reasoning is incorrect because one physical characteristic (such as a landform) and one human characteristic (such as an activity) make a description complete, even if the climate and buildings are not mentioned.
The reasoning is correct because a description without climate information is always incomplete.
The reasoning is incorrect because climate is a human characteristic and should not be part of a geographic description.
hints: The lesson shows that the check has only two questions, not three. What does each question ask for?
The worked example shows that naming one physical detail and one human detail is enough—no third kind of detail is required.

problemText: A geographer examines three descriptions of a mountain town called Slate Ridge. Description 1: 'Slate Ridge is built high in a mountain pass where winters are long and snowy.' Description 2: 'Slate Ridge has narrow streets lined with stone buildings, and miners work in tunnels beneath the town.' Description 3: 'Slate Ridge sits in a mountain pass with a cool, dry climate. The town square holds a weekly market where local crafts are sold.' The geographer says that only one of these descriptions can be made complete by adding a single detail. Which description is that, and what kind of detail would complete it?
choices: Description 1 would be complete with the addition of any human characteristic, such as a building or an activity.
Description 2 would be complete with the addition of any physical characteristic, such as a landform or a climate description.
Description 3 is already complete and needs nothing added to it.
None of these descriptions can be made complete by adding just one detail because they are all too vague.
hints: First check each description against the two-question routine. Description 3 mentions a mountain pass (landform), climate (climate), and a weekly market (activity). Does it pass both questions?
Remember: completeness requires at least one physical characteristic and at least one human characteristic. Once both are named, the description is complete—adding more details does not change that.

problemText: A student reads this sentence: 'Perception is how one particular person understands or describes a place, built from that person's own experience.' Based on the lesson, which statement about perception is correct?
choices: Perception is the same for everyone who visits a place because all people naturally see the same physical features and remember them in the same way.
Perception depends on whether a person is smart enough to notice details that other people miss when they visit places.
Perception comes from what each individual person has actually experienced, not from the place itself changing.
Perception is most accurate when it comes from someone who has studied the place in a book rather than visiting it in person.
hints: Look for the choice that matches the definition taught in the lesson about where perception comes from.
The lesson says perception is built from experience — not from book knowledge or being smart.

problemText: In the invented town of Hartwell, a resident named Omar lives on a street where a loud factory operates every weekday morning. He says, 'The street is not very loud.' A visitor spending one Saturday night there says, 'What a quiet, peaceful street!' Both people are describing the same street. Based on the lesson, why do their descriptions not match?
choices: One of them is not paying close attention and must be making a mistake.
The visitor is lying to make the street sound better than it really is.
Omar's weekday routine at this location has made the factory noise feel ordinary to him, while the visitor experienced the street on a quiet night and has no routine there yet.
The street actually changes how loud it is depending on who is walking on it.
hints: Think about what experiences Omar and the visitor have actually had on this street — not about who they are as people.
The lesson teaches that a resident's routine can make things feel ordinary, and a visitor might see a place at a different time or without routine experience.

problemText: A student is reading two descriptions of the same city market: (1) A person who works in the market six days a week says, 'This market is an ordinary shopping place.' (2) A person visiting the city for the first time says, 'The market is crowded and dazzling — there are smells and colors everywhere!' The student thinks one of these people must be wrong. Based on the lesson, is the student correct?
choices: No. Both people are accurately reporting what their own experience of the market actually was, and neither description is more correct than the other.
Yes, because the person who works there every day has learned the market better through repeated visits and must be describing it more truthfully than a visitor.
Yes, because a first-time visitor always notices more important details about a place than someone whose daily routine has made them overlook things.
No, because the market changes its layout and inventory too frequently for any two different people to make stable observations about it.
hints: The lesson teaches the 'equal-validity rule' — check what that means about which person's description is more correct.
Think about what each person has experienced: one has routine experience, one has newness experience. Can both be accurate at the same time?

problemText: In the invented village of Brookside, a resident named Yuki walks the same hilly path to school almost every day. She describes it as 'a normal path with some ups and downs.' A visitor named Marcus, who grew up in a completely flat region where there are no hills at all, walks the same path for the first time and says, 'This path is incredibly steep and exhausting.' Why do the lesson concepts suggest their perceptions differ?
choices: Yuki is a faster and stronger walker than Marcus, so the physical effort required to climb hills does not affect her perception of the path's difficulty.
Marcus's point of comparison is flat land from his home region, so the same path feels much steeper to him than to Yuki, whose routine experience has made the hills feel ordinary.
Yuki is being deliberately polite and understating the actual steepness of the path because she does not want Marcus to feel discouraged or upset.
The path is actually constructed at two different steepnesses depending on which direction you walk it and the time of day each person chose to walk it.
hints: Find the choice that explains their different perceptions using stated experience — what each person is used to at home, and how often they have walked this path.
The lesson teaches about 'point of comparison' — what place is each person already used to measuring things against?

problemText: A student is explaining why a resident and a visitor describe their town's river differently. The student writes: 'The visitor says the river is beautiful and amazing because she is more observant than the resident. The resident does not say the river is beautiful because he does not notice beauty the way visitors do.' Based on the lesson, what is wrong with this explanation?
choices: It correctly explains the difference but uses the wrong word — 'beautiful' instead of 'amazing.'
It traces the difference to who the people are (how observant or sensitive they are) instead of tracing it to each person's stated experience with the river.
It fails to mention that rivers are usually more beautiful in the spring than in other seasons.
It incorrectly assumes that residents think about rivers, when actually residents never think about the places they live.
hints: The lesson teaches how to explain differences in perception: point to stated experience, not to what kind of person someone is.
A good explanation should mention things like routine, how long someone has been there, or what they are used to comparing things to — not personality traits.

problemText: Read this scenario: In the town of Millstone, a resident named Teo lives on a street where there is a small, old library. He walks past it every morning on his way to work and calls it 'unremarkable — just an old building.' A visitor named Sofia, who is from a town with no public library, walks past the same library for the first time and says, 'What an incredible place! I have never seen anything like it.' A student offers three possible explanations: (1) Teo is not smart enough to appreciate the library; (2) Sofia's home town being without a library makes this one feel special to her by comparison, and Teo's daily routine has made it feel ordinary; (3) The library is actually beautiful only on days when visitors come. Which explanation best uses the lesson concepts?
choices: Explanation 1, because Teo has lived there longer and should understand the library better.
Explanation 2, because it traces each person's perception to their stated experience — Sofia's point of comparison and Teo's routine.
Explanation 3, because it acknowledges that places change depending on who is looking at them.
All three explanations are equally valid because perception is individual.
hints: Review the lesson's core teaching about how to explain differences in perception — should you use who people are, or should you use their stated experience?
Test each explanation by asking: Does it trace back to something stated about how each person has experienced the place, or does it make a claim about the people themselves?

problemText: When you compare two places, you need to match the same kind of characteristic on both sides. Which pair shows a correctly matched comparison?
choices: Comparing one place's mountains to another place's wheat farming
Comparing one place's cold winters to another place's wooden buildings
Comparing one place's tall buildings to another place's river valley
Comparing one place's climate to another place's climate
hints: Remember: physical characteristics go with physical, and human characteristics go with human.
Look for two characteristics that are the same KIND, not two characteristics from different places.

problemText: Lakeside sits on flat land next to a large lake and has cool summers. Most people there build houses with large windows to let in light. Hilltown sits on steep, rocky slopes and has cool summers too. Most people there build houses with small, thick walls to stay warm. Which sentence is a genuine similarity between these two places?
choices: Both Lakeside and Hilltown have cool summers
Lakeside has flat land while Hilltown has steep slopes
Lakeside's houses have large windows but Hilltown's houses have small, thick walls
Lakeside is next to water but Hilltown is in the mountains
hints: A similarity means both places share the same kind of characteristic, and that characteristic is the same in both.
Check each choice: does it describe the same kind of characteristic for both places, and is that characteristic alike in both?

problemText: Plainville stretches across wide, open grassland with very dry summers. Forestholm lies in a thick forest region with very dry summers as well. Plainville's residents grow grain crops, while Forestholm's residents cut timber for building. Which sentence correctly states a difference between these two places?
choices: Plainville grows grain, so it has better summers than Forestholm
Plainville sits on grassland while Forestholm sits in a forest
Plainville's summers are drier because it is not surrounded by trees
Forestholm cuts timber, which means it has different landforms than Plainville
hints: A difference compares the same kind of characteristic and shows how they are NOT alike.
Check which choice matches a physical characteristic with a physical characteristic — not a landform with an activity.

problemText: A student writes: "Porttown has a busy harbor where ships dock every day, while Mountainview has tall peaks. Therefore, Porttown's location is much different from Mountainview's location." This statement has a problem. Which correction fixes it?
choices: The student should remove the word 'much' so the statement sounds more objective
The student should say that Porttown is a better place because harbors bring more visitors
The student should describe Mountainview's location (a coastal plain or a mountainside) instead of just naming its landform, so the comparison matches location with location
The student should compare Porttown's activity (ships docking) to Mountainview's activity (mining or farming), instead of comparing a human characteristic to a physical characteristic
hints: The error is mixing a human characteristic (busy harbor with ships) with a physical characteristic (tall peaks). What should be compared instead?
Both places have a location — their overall setting. What is Porttown's location or setting? What is Mountainview's location or setting?

problemText: Desert Town has hot, dry summers and winters, and its people live in low, thick-walled buildings made of clay. Garden Town has mild, cool summers and mild, cool winters, and its people live in tall wooden houses with many windows. A student compares the two towns and says: "Desert Town's weather is much harsher, so Garden Town must be the better place to live." Why is this statement wrong as a geography comparison?
choices: Because Desert Town actually has milder weather than Garden Town
Because the student did not look at both places' buildings in addition to their weather
Because a difference in climate does not make one place better or worse — it just makes them different
Because the student should have mentioned that Desert Town's buildings are made of clay instead of wood
hints: The error is not about whether one place is better. Reread the lesson rule about comparisons and ranking.
A comparison can correctly identify a difference, but what does the lesson say about turning a difference into a rank or judgment?

problemText: Coastal Landing sits on a sandy shore with warm, wet summers and is flooded by rain and storm surge each year. Its buildings are built on tall stilts. Most people work as fishers. Dry Ridge sits on a high, rocky plateau with warm, dry summers and rarely sees rain. Its buildings are built close to the ground with deep foundations. Most people work as herders. A student is asked to find a genuine similarity and a genuine difference between the two places. The student writes: "Both places have warm summers, which is a similarity. Their buildings are different because Coastal Landing uses stilts while Dry Ridge uses deep foundations." Is this comparison correct?
choices: Yes, because both statements correctly match the same kind of characteristic on each side and accurately describe what the lesson said about each place
No, because warm summers are not truly the same when one place experiences wet conditions and the other experiences dry conditions, making the climate pattern fundamentally different
No, because the student identified a building style difference when the lesson shows that the real difference lies in how precipitation and landform shape construction choices differently
No, because the student should have compared how each place's geography affects the types of work people do rather than comparing physical features like climate and building styles
hints: Check each statement: does it match physical-with-physical or human-with-human? Does it accurately describe what was said about each place?
For the first statement, look at the descriptions again: does Coastal Landing have warm, wet summers? Does Dry Ridge have warm, dry summers? Is 'both have warm summers' what the descriptions say?

problemText: When you sketch and label a community map, what do you add to each landmark that a mental map does not have?
choices: A label that identifies whether the landmark is physical or human
A compass rose showing north, south, east, and west directions
A distance scale showing how many miles apart the landmarks are
A color code that matches each landmark to a different neighborhood
hints: Think about what makes a community map different from just remembering the route in your head.
The lesson says a community map 'adds one more piece to each landmark: a label.'

problemText: A student is sketching a community map that includes a tall oak tree standing alone in a field. Which label should the student write next to the oak tree?
choices: Human, because trees are important landmarks in a community and must be labeled to show their significance to residents
Physical, because the tree occurs on its own without being built or added by people
Human, because someone planted the tree in that location years ago, making it a landmark created through human action
Physical, because it is old and has been there a long time, which means it developed naturally over many years
hints: Remember: physical landmarks occur on their own; human landmarks are built or added by people.
Even if a person planted it long ago, does that mean the tree itself is something people built or constructed?

problemText: A student's labeled map of River Town shows these landmarks in order: town hall (human), small pond (physical), park gate (human), rocky outcrop (physical). When the student checks this map against the written description, the order of landmarks and all the turns match perfectly. What should the student conclude about this labeled map?
choices: The map is wrong because it has too many physical landmarks
The map is wrong because the turns do not match the description
The map is correctly labeled because the order and turns match the description
The map needs to be redrawn because a park gate is actually a physical landmark
hints: The lesson says that getting the order and turns right is separate from labeling correctly.
If the order and all the turns match the description, and each label fits what the landmark actually is, then what is the verdict?

problemText: A student sketches a map of Millbrook following this description: 'Starting at the library, go straight to a small waterfall. From the waterfall, turn to the town square. From the town square, turn to a gravel path.' The student's finished map shows the landmarks in the correct order with the correct turns, but labels them: library (human), waterfall (human), town square (human), gravel path (human). How many labels are incorrect, and which landmark or landmarks should be relabeled?
choices: One label is wrong: the waterfall should be physical
Two labels are wrong: the waterfall and the gravel path should be physical
Three labels are wrong: the waterfall, the town square, and the gravel path should be physical
All four labels are wrong and the entire map must be redrawn
hints: Go through each landmark one at a time and ask: did people build or add this, or does it occur on its own?
A waterfall, a town square, a gravel path — think carefully about which ones are features people created and which occur naturally.

problemText: A student describes a community map out loud: 'From the fire station (human), straight ahead to Pine Creek (physical); turn left to the covered bridge (human); turn right to a sandy beach (physical) at the water's edge.' When the student sketches this map and checks it against the description, the order, turns, and labels all match. What can the student confidently say about this labeled community map?
choices: The map is correctly labeled and ready to present because every landmark is in the right place with the right label
The map must be wrong because a covered bridge is too small to be considered an important landmark on most community maps
The map cannot be checked yet because it does not include the student's neighborhood name or other residential streets
The map needs revision because Pine Creek should be labeled human since streams and creeks are often managed by communities
hints: The lesson teaches you to check one landmark at a time: the name, the turn, and whether its label is physical or human.
If the order, turns, and physical-or-human labels all match the description, what does that tell you?

problemText: A student's friend creates a labeled map of Ashwood from this description: 'Starting at the schoolhouse, a path leads straight ahead to a large ravine. From the ravine, a turn leads to the community center. From the community center, another turn leads to an old wooden dock.' The friend's labels read: schoolhouse (human), ravine (physical), community center (human), dock (human). The student is asked to check this map. The student notices that the order and turns match the description perfectly. However, when the student rechecks the description to confirm whether 'dock' should be labeled physical or human, the student realizes this label might be wrong. Why might the dock label be incorrect, even though the order and turns are right?
choices: Because a dock is constructed by people as a structure built into or over the water, making it a human landmark rather than a physical one
Because a dock is a structure people built or added, so it should be labeled human, which matches the friend's label and is correct
Because the description does not provide enough detail about whether the dock was originally built by people or formed naturally over time
Because a dock must be very old if it is wooden, so it should be labeled as a historical feature that does not fit either the physical or human category
hints: Think about what a dock is: is it something that occurs on its own in nature, or something people built?
The friend labeled the dock as human. Is that label correct based on what a dock actually is?
